extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematical students, and contributors/readers of a 19th-century mathematical problems journal
extracted.subtask_short: solving classical geometry and algebra exercises
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of worked solutions and methods for classical geometry and algebra problems (reciprocal surfaces, conics, loci, polygon constructions, cubic discriminant, etc.) as presented in a mathematical-journal 'Solutions of Mathematical Exercises' section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method choice for reciprocal surfaces (geometric vs algebraic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The geometrical mode of investigation, although admirably suited to prove the general properties of reciprocal surfaces, is not competent to find the equation of one of the surfaces when that of the other is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer an algebraic approach when the task is to find the explicit equation of a reciprocal polar surface given the other; geometric methods are appropriate for proving general properties but insufficient for explicit equation-finding. (From Scholium: 'The geometrical mode of investigation ... is not competent to find the equation ... This problem being solved, the theory of reciprocal surfaces is complete.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult canonical references when unfamiliar with a method
rubrics_metrics.description: If the student is not acquainted with the geometrical method of exhibiting the theory of reciprocal polars, consult primary sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Poncelet's 'Mémoire sur la théorie générale des polaires reciproques' and Chasles' 'Memoir on sphere polar reciprocals' for the geometrical method and foundational material. (Text: 'The sttident who is not acquainted ... is referred to Poncelet ... and to Chasles ...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive loci by coordinate representation and elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up coordinate equations (of surfaces/tangents/normals), express tangent-plane equations via directing cosines, impose orthogonality constraints, and eliminate the unknown direction-cosine variables to obtain the locus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As in CLXXV: denote directing cosines of normals; write tangent plane equations (equations (4),(5),(6)); use orthogonality relations (sums/products of direction cosines) and add/square/eliminate to obtain the locus (resulting sphere). Follow a systematic algebraic elimination procedure rather than geometric intuition when an explicit locus is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use centre-based constructions for inscribed spherical polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: To inscribe a spherical polygon whose great-circle planes must pass through given points, draw lines from the centre to the given points, intersect those with the given plane, and construct the polygon in that plane; then the planes through the centre and those polygon edges yield the required great-circle arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same construction to second-order surfaces (provided the given plane is not diametral) and generalize by replacing diametral sections with sections through any given point not in the given plane. (From Lhuilier solution: construction and extension notes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide multiple solutions and enumerate corollaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply more than one valid solution approach when possible and list immediate corollaries and further properties that follow from the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show first, second, third solutions for the same exercise and enumerate corollaries (A)-(F) and other properties. Present alternative methods (synthetic, analytic, trigonometric), then derive corollaries and related identities/relations to illustrate consequences and strengthen understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform to standard forms and use discriminants for root-nature criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: For polynomial/root-nature problems, transform the general equation into a depressed/standard form and apply known discriminant/cardano/Sturm criteria to determine whether roots are real, equal, or imaginary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (cubic): reduce to depressed cubic, express Cardan's expression B^2 + (4/27)A^3 etc., and compare 1 SaW ... with 4ca^+4^^+27c^ (text paraphrase) to decide whether all roots are real and unequal, two equal, or two imaginary. Show the algebraic manipulations explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and use symmetry or limiting/special-case arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, exploit symmetries, special parameter values, or limit cases to simplify equations or deduce the form/nature of solutions (e.g., surfaces of revolution, principal vertices at origin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: when coordinate axes are principal, impose Ai = Aj ... and Bi = 0 to simplify reciprocal surface equations; when parameters take special values reduce general equations to planes or umbilical surfaces. Explicitly state which special-case assumptions are being used and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge contributors and indicate multiple acceptable solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Record and attribute alternate valid solutions submitted by various correspondents and indicate when multiple respondents produced correct or useful variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal lists 'Good solutions were also received from …' after many exercises; follow this practice to credit contributors and to show that multiple solution forms are acceptable and valued.
